title: Income Statement: the profit-and-loss report
subtitle: From revenue down to net income - the story of efficiency
openingQuestion: Where does the Income Statement start, and where does it end?
openingOptions: From equity all the way down to the dividends paid out
From revenue (top line) to net income (bottom line)
explanation: The income statement runs from revenue at the very top down to net income at the very bottom, subtracting each group of costs in a deliberate order: direct costs first, operating costs next, then interest and tax. That order lets you isolate the problem - a shrinking gross margin is a production or pricing issue, a shrinking operating margin is an issue with the business's cost structure, and a falling net income while both margins above it stay steady points to debt.

diagram.label: Revenue sits at the very top
Each group of costs is subtracted in turn
Each layer produces a different kind of profit
Down to net income at the very bottom

realWorldExample.description: FPT's income statement is a clear example of this layered structure: consolidated revenue comes from three segments (Technology, Telecom, Education); after subtracting cost of goods sold you get Gross Profit; after subtracting selling and administrative expenses you get Operating Income; after subtracting interest expense and corporate income tax (usually around 20%) you get Net Income. FPT's net margin has held around 10-13% for several years running, reflecting a technology-services model with a far steadier margin than capital-intensive manufacturers.

quiz.question: Which line does the Income Statement start from?
options: Cost of goods sold
Gross Profit
Revenue
Interest expense
quiz.explanation: P&L: Revenue - COGS - OpEx - Interest - Tax = Net Income. Revenue is the very first line.

quiz.question: What is the very last line of the Income Statement?
options: Gross Profit
Operating Income
EBITDA (before interest, tax, and depreciation)
Net Income
quiz.explanation: Net Income is the final profit remaining after every expense (COGS, OpEx, Interest, Tax).

quiz.question: Why does the Income Statement matter?
options: It shows whether the business turned a profit or a loss from operations in the period
It shows how many assets the company owns and how much it owes
It shows how much real cash actually moved in and out during the period
It shows the ownership structure and the stakes held by major shareholders
quiz.explanation: Net Income and profit margins reflect operating efficiency. A profitable company reflects core business health.

quiz.question: What is the difference between Operating Income and Net Income?
options: Operating has already subtracted depreciation, Net has not
Operating has not yet subtracted interest and tax, Net has subtracted both
Operating is measured on a cash basis, Net on an accrual basis
Operating counts only core revenue, while Net also adds in secondary and non-operating revenue
quiz.explanation: Operating = profit from core operations before interest/tax. Net = profit after interest/tax. Operating reflects business performance; Net reflects shareholder profit.

quiz.question: A company has a 20% Operating Margin but only a 12% Net Margin. What explains the gap?
options: Selling and administrative costs are above the industry average
Rising cost of goods sold has squeezed the gross margin
Interest expense and tax have eaten up 8 percentage points
Revenue is recognised on an accrual basis, so cash hasn't been collected yet
quiz.explanation: A high Operating Margin but low Net Margin means the company is profitable at the operating level but interest or high taxes are eating into it further down.

quiz.question: What is EBITDA?
options: Gross profit after subtracting selling and administrative expenses
After-tax profit with dividends paid added back on top
Net cash flow generated from operations during the period
Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation, and amortisation
quiz.explanation: EBITDA = Operating Income + Depreciation/Amortisation. It strips out non-cash expenses and the effects of financing and tax, making it useful for comparing companies.

quiz.question: If you want to compare the profitability of two companies with different capital structures, which metric should you use?
options: Operating Income or EBITDA
Each company's Net Income
Net Margin, expressed as a percentage
After-tax profit divided by average shareholders' equity
quiz.explanation: Net Income is affected by capital structure and tax. Operating Income/EBITDA give a cleaner comparison of the actual businesses.

quiz.question: A company has positive net income but negative Operating Income. Can that actually happen?
options: No, Net can never be larger than Operating in any case
Yes, if there is an unusual gain, such as from selling an asset
No, this is definitely an accounting error
Yes, but only when the company is exempt from income tax
quiz.explanation: Net Income = Operating + Non-operating items. If non-operating gains exceed the operating loss, Net Income can still be positive - though this signals a weak core business.

quiz.question: How does seasonality affect the Income Statement?
options: It only affects the balance sheet, not the income statement
Revenue between quarters always stays stable for a good business
Revenue swings with the season, so you must compare against the same period last year
Comparing only against the immediately preceding quarter is enough to see the real trend
quiz.explanation: A company that sells Tet goods sees high Q1 and low Q3 sales. You need a year-over-year (YoY) comparison to understand the real trend.

quiz.question: Between Operating Income and Net Income, which one do investors usually care about more?
options: Operating Income, because it reflects core business strength before any debt effects
Net Income, because it's the final figure left after every single expense and tax is subtracted
EBITDA, because it strips out the effect of depreciation policy
Both equally, since they always move in the same direction
quiz.explanation: Operating = core business health. Net = also depends on debt/tax. Investors prefer a high Operating figure, since that reflects real growth potential.

quiz.question: Two companies in the same industry have equal Revenue, but one has far more 'non-recurring' costs on its Income Statement. How does that affect comparing their Net Income?
options: Non-recurring items should be stripped out before comparing the two
The company with more non-recurring costs is always the less efficient one
Equal revenue means the two are directly comparable as-is
Net Income always reflects a company's true underlying efficiency
quiz.explanation: Unusual items (impairment, asset disposals, restructuring costs) distort a given period's Net Income. Analysts typically normalise for these to compare the companies' true, repeatable operating performance.

keyTakeaways: The P&L runs from Revenue down to Net Income
Each layer reflects a different aspect of operating efficiency
Top line = Revenue; Bottom line = Net Income

practicePrompt.question: A company has Revenue of 1,000 billion, and after subtracting COGS, operating costs, interest, and tax in turn, is left with Net Income of 80 billion. What principle does this P&L structure express?
options: The P&L is a list of independent line items with no logical order between them
The P&L runs from Revenue down to Net Income, with each tier subtracting another distinct kind of cost
Revenue and Net Income must always be equal if a company is well managed and has no unusual costs
Net Income is simply a fixed 8% of Revenue that applies to every company
practicePrompt.explanation: The P&L runs from Revenue (top line) down to Net Income (bottom line) layer by layer: subtracting COGS gives Gross Profit, subtracting SG&A/R&D gives Operating Income, subtracting interest and tax gives Net Income - each layer reveals a different aspect of efficiency: production, operations, and capital structure.

summary.keyIdea: The P&L runs from Revenue down to Net Income
summary.commonMistake: Reading a concept as a phrase to memorise rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: Each layer reflects a different aspect of operating efficiency

application.title: Trace a company's Revenue down to its Net Income
application.message: Take a company you're interested in, follow its Income Statement line by line from Revenue down to Net Income, and note down what each deduction represents.
application.secondary: Doing this slowly, one line at a time, is enough to remember the P&L structure for good.

sections.text: If the Balance Sheet is a photograph, the Income Statement is a short film telling the story of how a business earned and spent money over a quarter or a year. Reading a P&L correctly means understanding what each layer of profit is telling you.
The layered structure of the Income Statement

The P&L is not one single number but a chain of profit layers, each subtracting a different kind of cost. Starting from Revenue (the top line), subtract Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) to get Gross Profit; subtract Operating Expenses (SG&A, R&D) to get Operating Income (EBIT); subtract Interest Expense to get Earnings Before Tax (EBT); subtract Tax Expense to get Net Income (the bottom line).
Why look at every layer, not just Net Income

Two companies with equal Net Income can have completely different stories. One may reach a high Net Income through a strong Gross Margin (products with real pricing power), while the other reaches the same Net Income by cutting operating costs or through a one-off unusual gain. Looking at each layer helps an investor tell sustainable profit apart from a one-time boost.

items: Revenue (Top line): the total value of goods/services sold during the period.
Gross Profit = Revenue − COGS: profit after the direct cost of production.
Operating Income (EBIT) = Gross Profit − OpEx: profit from core business operations.
Net Income (Bottom line) = EBIT − Interest − Tax: the final profit belonging to shareholders.

sections.label: A quick-read tip
sections.text: When reading an unfamiliar company's P&L, calculate the margin at every layer (Gross Margin, Operating Margin, Net Margin) and compare it with the same period last year or with an industry peer - a sharp swing in margin is usually a signal worth digging into.
